statement_nl: Let $p$ be a prime number greater than $3$. For each $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-1\\}$, let $I(k) \\in \\{1,2,\\dots,p-1\\}$ be such that $k \\cdot I(k) \\equiv 1 \\pmod{p}$. Prove that the number of integers $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-2\\}$ such that $I(k+1) < I(k)$ is greater than $p/4-1$.

domain_restrictions: p is an integer prime and p > 3 (so p ≥ 5)
k ranges over integers; when defining I(k) we take k ∈ {1,...,p-1} so gcd(k,p)=1 and multiplicative inverse exists and is unique in {1,...,p-1}
The counting index k for the inequality I(k+1) < I(k) is restricted to k ∈ {1,...,p-2} so that k+1 ∈ {2,...,p-1} (all inverses involved are defined)
Counts such as |S| are nonnegative integers
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every prime p > 3, define I: {1,...,p-1} -> {1,...,p-1} by I(k) being the unique integer with k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p). Let S = { k ∈ {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then |S| > p/4 - 1. Equivalently (since |S| is integral), |S| ≥ floor(p/4).
quantifier_order: For all primes p with p > 3 (p is fixed for the rest of the statement)
For all k in {1,...,p-1}, there exists a unique I(k) in {1,...,p-1} with k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p) (uniqueness follows from p prime and gcd(k,p)=1)
Define S = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }
Claim: |S| > p/4 - 1 (equivalently, |S| ≥ floor(p/4) since |S| is an integer)

variables.domain: explicitly ranges over {1,2,...,p-1} when defining I(k); the count is taken over k in {1,2,...,p-2}
variables.name: k
variables.role: index variable for inverses and for the counted property

variables.name: I
variables.role: map sending k to its multiplicative inverse modulo p, i.e. I(k) is the unique integer in 1..p-1 with k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p)

variables.name: S
variables.role: S = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }, the set being counted

witness_dependencies: I(k) is a deterministic function of k and the fixed prime p; i.e. witness I(k) depends on (k,p)
I(k+1) depends on k and p via I applied to k+1; thus the predicate I(k+1) < I(k) depends on k and p
The uniqueness of I(k) is guaranteed by p being prime (implicit use of gcd(k,p)=1)
The set S (and its cardinality) depends on p through I
